source_excerpt: Anna proposed engraving her initials on the base of the new glasswork so that future repairs might be traced to the proper maker. I said manufacturers had survived for centuries without turning every joint into a monument. Voss produced one of my first blue ledgers and showed me where I had complained of unacknowledged work at twenty. I accused them both of conspiring against a harmless preference for visual cleanliness. Anna offered to make the mark small enough that only a repairer could see it. I agreed. Six weeks later the mark allowed us to identify which batch of joints had a slight internal defect. I wrote to Anna congratulating her on the usefulness of the mark and said nothing about our original disagreement. It had been settled, after all, by data. She returned the letter with the word 'naturally' pencilled beneath my signature.

source_excerpt: A merchant whose son had lost the use of an arm sought me out through Reuter. He had heard that I made living bodies where ordinary doctors found only damage. I was tempted to offer a grand account of my accomplishments. Reuter asked me to explain what I could actually do for the boy. I had no treatment to offer, and the father was not interested in a lecture on the future of science. We discussed a brace being prepared by a local craftsman, then let him go. Later, Voss said she had never heard me speak so little to a paying visitor. I replied that he had come seeking medicine, not philosophy, and I did not possess the commodity he required. His disappointment was sharper than most committee judgments. I do not claim it improved me. I remember that he thanked Reuter and did not thank me.

source_excerpt: Rosa Brandl arrived with coal in a cart that shed black water over my threshold. I asked her to place three baskets beneath the east stairs and she declined until she had inspected the floor. It was rotten, she said, and she would not have the collapse of an aristocratic ruin attributed to her horse. I informed her that the place possessed no aristocracy except the intellectual kind. She placed the coal in the kitchen instead, where its dust settled upon my clean papers. Her measure was tin, deeply dented, and indisputably honest. I paid more than I had intended, then watched her carry the final basket without the assistance I had neglected to offer. For three winters afterward she knew my fuel expenditure more accurately than any surviving colleague knew my work. She never called me Professor. Curiously, I did not correct her.

source_excerpt: The seaweed arrived leaking brine through three layers of paper and a courier's protest. From it, by means I shall not publish, came the Mermaid. She occupied her watery chamber in such perfect stillness that I feared a beautiful failure. Clara discovered that she moved when visitors departed. We watched from behind a screen, uncomfortably bent like burglars in our own laboratory, while the little figure rose and vanished among the weed. I wrote 'timid' in the ledger. It remains possible that she was timid, and equally possible that she possessed an excellent opinion of the advantages of avoiding me.

I agreed, not wishing to seem a barbarian in a lady's house. Reuter spent the meal describing an elderly patient who stole pears from his own orchard because he no longer recognized its new owner. source_excerpt: During a lean month I preserved enough money for lamp oil by economizing on supper. Clara discovered this when she found bread hardened beside the sink and my hands shaking while I tried to set a stopcock. She said I was unfit to handle delicate glass until I had eaten. I accused her of treating me like a patient; she replied that patients occasionally possessed the sense to follow instructions. Later that evening a farm boy brought a parcel of food from Lenz's household and refused a tip. I gave him my portion of cheese for the road, then regretted it before he reached the gate. I ate the bread and preserved the lamps. There was no nobility in the transaction. The following day my hands were steady and the experiment behaved. I began keeping provisions near the workroom, which I represented to visitors as a contribution to experimental reliability rather than obedience to Clara.

source_excerpt: Leonie produced a crown small enough for the Queen, using fine wire and a red glass bead Lenz had rejected as imperfect. It was beautifully made. I rewarded the gift with an inventory of its historical errors, then carried it to the laboratory in a cotton-lined box. The Queen stood beneath it for several moments without attempting to take it. When I opened the cabinet the following morning, the crown lay behind a feeding dish. I accused Lenz of having brushed it aside. He showed me where the Queen had dragged it herself, leaving a trail in the damp medium. Leonie laughed when I told her. She asked whether the Queen was a more discerning patron than I. I said she had the same intolerable inclination to judge a gift by whether she wanted it. Nevertheless, before returning the crown to its box I repaired the bent wire myself. I took uncommon care with a thing its intended owner appeared to dislike.

source_excerpt: I wrote to Jolivet demanding that he distinguish the proposed reproduction of organized life from any claim that I had accomplished it. He replied with courtesy and pointed to the very paragraph in which he had already made that distinction. There was nothing to correct. I held the letter near the lamp, where the watermark showed through, searching for an insolent expression. I found none. I wrote a second letter about his insinuations concerning responsibility, one whose severity would have done honor to an unhappy prosecutor. It remained on my desk unsent. What I wanted, as I knew even then, was not merely a correction in the newspaper. I wanted another of those unhurried conversations in which he had seemed to find me amusing and important. The letter requested no such thing. At last I put his answer among my offprints. I told myself I had preserved the evidence of his journalistic cunning. I had also preserved his handwriting.

source_excerpt: The brass lever had once responded cleanly to the slightest pressure. Now it caught at an angle and stained the thumb with grease. Lenz proposed a new fitting. I rejected it for want of funds, then discovered that the worn motion repeated more faithfully than the newer apparatus beside it. We measured the deviation and marked the handle with a black line. After that I could feel the small resistance through the glove before reading the scale. The instrument had acquired a character. Lenz called this the ordinary life of machinery. I objected to such undisciplined personification while returning to the same handle each morning. When the leather grip finally split, I had him replace the leather and preserve the metal. He shook his head and did exactly as I requested, which was, I believe, the first time he obeyed an instruction without argument.

source_excerpt: An editor from Augsburg returned our prospectus with the assurance that claims of miniature men could be dismissed without an inspection. He had, however, complimented my literary manner, which showed him capable of good judgment in a narrow field. Mathilde had already composed a rebuttal before I arrived. She proposed to print the rejection beside an inventory of witnessed behaviors. I advised her that humiliation was more effective when administered sparingly; she replied that I had furnished enough for a lifetime. We quarrelled over whether the editor's name belonged on the sheet. She wished to print it. I did not wish to give a mediocrity the immortality of appearing in my pamphlet. In the end we printed the inventory alone, with empty spaces where independent corroboration might someday be placed. I enjoyed imagining him discovering those spaces and mistaking them for mercy.

source_excerpt: A letter from Theodor arrived after years in which our correspondence had dwindled to notes at Christmas. He had secured a position supervising architectural drawings and was living with a man whose patience, he said, exceeded that of most professors. The sentence was not an accusation, though I spent a whole afternoon searching it for one. He enclosed a photograph of a building whose windows he had designed. It was handsome and insufficiently ventilated. I prepared a reply listing the defect, then put the sheet away. Clara, bringing fresh cloth for the jars, found me looking at the picture. I told her that the work was competently done. She asked whether I had said as much to him. I wrote him three sentences of praise and an additional paragraph about the windows. He answered in kind, correcting a detail I had misunderstood about the plan. We had lost the ease of our earlier life. We had not lost the pleasure of being exact together.
